title: Ozempic Users Are Exercising Less, Not More. For South Asians, That Is a Dangerous Trade-Off.
excerpt: A study of 753 GLP-1 users found daily steps fell 11 per cent and active minutes dropped 21 per cent after starting treatment. Muscle loss is the hidden cost.
body:
The promise was simple: lose the weight, gain the energy, start moving more. For the millions of people now taking GLP-1 medications like Ozempic, Wegovy, and Mounjaro, the assumption that shedding pounds would naturally lead to a more active life seemed almost self-evident.

A study presented this weekend at ENDO 2026, the Endocrine Society's annual meeting in Chicago, says the opposite is happening. People on GLP-1 drugs are exercising less, not more — and for South Asians, who face some of the highest rates of diabetes and visceral obesity in the world, the implications deserve serious attention.

The Numbers

Researchers led by Dr Sajana Maharjan of HSHS St. John's Hospital in Springfield, Illinois, analysed data from the National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program, which links electronic health records with Fitbit activity data. Among 1,950 adults with obesity who started a GLP-1 medication, 753 had enough wearable data for meaningful analysis.

The findings were stark. Average daily steps fell from 5,047 to 4,487 after starting treatment — a decline of more than 11 per cent. Moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) minutes dropped from 28 to 22 per day, a 21 per cent reduction. The largest declines occurred in men and in people with musculoskeletal pain.

"While many assume that weight loss leads naturally to increased physical activity, our study suggests otherwise," Dr Maharjan said. "Exercise cannot be optional for people taking these medications."

""While many assume that weight loss leads naturally to increased physical activity, our study suggests otherwise," Dr Maharjan said."

Why This Matters for South Asians

GLP-1 medications have become one of the most prescribed drug classes in the United States, and South Asian patients are a fast-growing segment of users. The community's well-documented predisposition to insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and central adiposity — often at BMIs that would be considered normal in other populations — makes these drugs appealing.

But here is the problem GLP-1s cannot solve on their own: they reduce fat and lean muscle mass. For South Asians, who already tend to carry less skeletal muscle relative to body fat, this creates a compounding vulnerability. Losing muscle while losing weight accelerates sarcopenia — age-related muscle wasting — and raises the risk of falls, fractures, and metabolic dysfunction down the line.

The clinical term for this is "sarcopenic obesity," and South Asians are among the populations most susceptible to it. A person can drop two clothing sizes and still be metabolically fragile if muscle loss outpaces fat loss.

The Fatigue Trap

Clinicians who treat South Asian patients on GLP-1s say the exercise decline is not surprising. "I often find that patients feel more fatigued while losing weight, which can make exercise feel like a chore," said Dr Mir Ali, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center in Fountain Valley, California.

The drugs suppress appetite — that is their core mechanism — and many users report nausea, reduced energy, and general malaise, particularly in the first months of treatment. For patients who were already sedentary, the reduced caloric intake can feel like permission to rest rather than a catalyst to move.

Another ENDO 2026 study, led by Sainikhil Sontha of Boston University, found that about 40 per cent of patients stop their GLP-1 medication within the first year, and nearly 60 per cent by year two. Among those who stop, more than half restart within a year — creating a pattern of metabolic yo-yoing that makes sustained exercise habits even harder to build.

What Diaspora Families Should Know

For NRI families considering or already using GLP-1 medications, the study carries a clear message: the drug is not a substitute for movement. The Endocrine Society's researchers are now calling for "targeted interventions" — structured exercise programmes bundled with prescriptions — to prevent muscle loss and ensure long-term metabolic health.

Practical steps matter more than clinical abstractions. Resistance training two to three times a week protects muscle. Walking 7,000 to 8,000 steps daily maintains cardiovascular function. Protein intake — a frequent blind spot in vegetarian South Asian diets — needs to be monitored when appetite is suppressed.

The weight may come off with a weekly injection. Keeping the body functional enough to enjoy that lighter frame requires something the drug cannot deliver: deliberate, sustained physical effort.
